questions.q: In the shared responsibility model, what does "security OF the cloud" refer to?
options: The customer's data and access configuration
The provider's responsibility for physical datacenters, host hardware, and the hypervisor
A legal contract term with no technical meaning
Antivirus software installed on the customer's virtual machines
questions.explain: Security OF the cloud is always the provider's job: physical security, host infrastructure, the hypervisor, and the network backbone.

questions.q: Which of the following is always the customer's responsibility, regardless of service model?
options: Guarding the physical datacenter
Patching the hypervisor
Managing their own data and identity/access controls
Maintaining the physical network backbone between regions
questions.explain: Data and identity/access management are security IN the cloud — always the customer's job, no matter which service model is in use.

questions.q: On an AWS RDS managed database, who patches the underlying operating system and database engine?
options: The customer, exactly as they would on a plain EC2 instance
AWS, since RDS manages the OS and database engine for the customer
Neither party — patching is unnecessary on managed databases
A third-party vendor unrelated to AWS
questions.explain: RDS is a managed database service: AWS patches the OS and database engine, while the customer manages the schema, data, and access.

questions.q: As you move from IaaS toward SaaS, what happens to the responsibility line between provider and customer?
options: It disappears entirely — SaaS has no shared responsibility model
It stays exactly the same across all three models
It shifts so the provider takes on more of the stack, while the customer still always keeps their data and identity management
It shifts so the customer takes on more responsibility
questions.explain: Moving from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS, the provider manages progressively more of the stack, but the customer's data and access management remain customer responsibilities throughout.

questions.q: A company's AWS access keys are leaked, and an attacker uses them to read data from a misconfigured S3 bucket. Under the shared responsibility model, whose fault is this?
options: AWS's fault, because the breach happened on their infrastructure
The customer's fault, because access control and credential security are security IN the cloud
Nobody's fault — this kind of incident can't be prevented
AWS's fault, because the hypervisor failed to isolate the customer's data
questions.explain: Access control, credential management, and bucket configuration are the customer's responsibility under security IN the cloud, which is why leaked keys and open buckets are the most common real-world cloud breaches.
